content: Marvel Electronics and Home Entertainment needs an online store to support the sale, distribution, and marketing of electronic products. Customers should be able to browse categorized product information, search the catalogue, and configure products from available components before ordering. The business also needs a way to present detailed product information and manage the customer-facing sales experience through the store.

The main goal is to grow sales by making it easier for customers to discover products, compare options, and place orders online without relying on the store team for every step. We also want the site to support marketing and product presentation, so it can showcase the catalogue properly and help move customers from browsing to purchase. On the business side, it should reduce friction in the sales process and give us a better online presence for electronics and home entertainment products.
In terms of customer journeys, we need to support a fairly simple browse-and-buy flow as well as more involved shopping where a customer searches, reads detailed specs, and configures a product from components before ordering. Some customers may know exactly what they want, while others will compare categories and versions before deciding. We also need to handle scenarios where the sale depends on product configuration or bundled components, since that’s a key part of how we sell these products.

I’d prioritize the core high-volume categories first, especially the products customers already expect to buy online, like TVs, audio equipment, and common home entertainment accessories. Those are the easiest to present clearly and should give us a strong first launch.
I’d probably hold back any categories that need a lot of explanation, special configuration, or more complex fulfillment until we’re confident the basics are working. If something needs a lot of setup or after-sales coordination, I’d rather not push that in the first phase.

That would mainly sit with the product or merchandising team, with input from sales and whoever handles inventory or operations. Pricing changes would usually come from commercial management, while availability would need to be checked against stock or supply. I’d expect those teams to coordinate through a clear approval process so updates go live without conflicting information, but I don’t know the exact workflow yet and would need to confirm it with the team.

We’d need the product manager or catalog administrator to handle the item details, categories, and descriptions. Sales or commercial staff would likely be responsible for pricing and promotional changes, while an operations or inventory person would keep availability and stock-related information current. In practice, a store manager might oversee the process and approve larger changes.

Day to day, people usually just say product or item for the thing being sold, and category for the group it belongs to. For pricing, they’d talk about the list price or selling price, and for promotions they’d usually say offer, discount, or special. For availability, the common terms would be in stock, out of stock, or available to order.

A bundle is usually a pre-set combination of products sold together as one offer, often at a better price than buying them separately. A variant is more like the same base product in different options, such as color, size, model, or specification. Components are the individual parts that can be selected or combined to build a product, so those are more flexible and usually need configuration rules to make sure the combination is valid.

We’d expect it to fit within our existing business systems as much as possible, especially whatever we use for inventory, pricing, and order handling, but I don’t have the exact platform decision yet. On compliance, we’d need the usual customer and payment protections, and anything related to consumer sales and warranty information would need to be shown clearly. Those boundaries mainly mean the store can’t promise stock or pricing that doesn’t match the back-end systems, and it has to present product and order information in a way that’s accurate and defensible.

Yes, we’d want anything that is supplier-provided or brand-sensitive to go through approval before it goes live, especially images and marketing copy. Some brands are strict about how their logos and names are displayed, so we’d need to follow their guidelines and not improvise. For certain products, we may also need to omit promotional wording or use only officially supplied content if that’s part of the agreement.

If a product page or search fails, I’d expect the store to show a clear error and let the customer continue browsing other areas rather than just breaking completely. If checkout fails, the priority would be to protect the order and payment process so the customer does not lose what they selected and can try again safely. We’d want the system to recover quickly, but I don’t have a formal uptime or disaster recovery target yet, so that would need to be agreed with the business and IT team.

For a customer-facing store, we’d generally expect it to be available most of the time, including evenings and weekends, because people shop outside office hours. I don’t have a formal SLA number agreed yet, but from a business point of view anything below very high availability would cause problems. If you need a target, I’d have to confirm that with IT and operations.

We’d prefer maintenance to happen late at night or during the lowest traffic period, and it should be kept as short as possible. I wouldn’t want it during weekends or public holiday periods if we can avoid it, since that’s when customers are more likely to browse. If downtime is unavoidable, we’d need clear notice beforehand and the impact kept to a minimum.

We’d want the core product catalogue details carried over, like product names, descriptions, categories, images, specifications, and pricing where it’s still valid. For marketing content, the main things are the approved banners, promotional copy, and any brand content that’s still current and allowed to be reused. The main goal is to avoid starting from scratch so the store can launch with enough content to sell properly and keep the brand consistent from day one.

I know some of it sits in our current product management records and some in the marketing team’s content files, but I don’t have the exact system names confirmed. There may also be supplier-provided files for certain ranges. I’d need to check with the team to give you the precise source systems.

Yes, definitely. For launch, we’d only want current, approved, and legally reusable content moved over, especially for the products we actually plan to sell first. Anything outdated, unapproved, or tied to old campaigns should be left behind or rebuilt properly, because we don’t want to carry across stale prices, expired promotions, or brand content that no longer fits.

Yes, ideally it should update as soon as possible so the customer isn’t surprised at checkout. If a price or stock level changes while they’re shopping, we’d rather show the current status and make it clear before they complete the order. If something changes at the last moment, the system should prompt them to confirm the updated price or availability rather than silently letting it go through.

For the first version, I’d expect the store to clearly show that it’s unavailable and stop the customer from completing that item as if it were in stock. If backorder is something the business wants to support, that would need to be an explicit decision, because it affects fulfilment and customer communication. A substitution could be useful later, but I wouldn’t assume it’s required unless the business signs off on it.

Yes, we’d expect the usual filters like price, brand, product type, and key specifications to be available wherever they make sense. Some categories will need special filters, though, because not every product type uses the same attributes, so the store should only show relevant options. I’d also want the system to avoid displaying empty or meaningless filters if there aren’t any products matching them.

Relevance should be the main thing, because customers need to find what they searched for quickly. After that, I’d expect available items to come before out-of-stock ones, and popular products could be boosted a bit if they’re equally relevant. I wouldn’t want margin to affect the default ranking unless the business specifically decides to do sponsored placement later.

We’d want them to feel fast and responsive, ideally just a couple of seconds at most for most searches and category views. If it starts taking much longer than that, customers will probably think the site is slow. I don’t have an exact performance target yet, but that’s the general expectation.

Yes, we should expect noticeable peaks during promotions, pay weekends, and holiday periods, and those are exactly the times customers will be searching and browsing the most. Catalogue size should also grow over time as we add more products and variants. So the search and browsing performance needs to hold up under those higher loads, not just on a quiet day.

Yes, for supplier or brand content we’d need it checked before going live, especially for product descriptions, images, logos, and any marketing copy that represents the brand. In some cases the supplier will insist we use the material exactly as provided, and in other cases we may need to follow their brand guidelines or not use it at all. If we don’t have the right approval or the content doesn’t meet the brand rules, it should stay off the storefront until it’s cleared.

It should tell them clearly what part of the configuration is invalid, in plain language, so they can understand what needs changing. If there’s a valid alternative, like a compatible component or a different package, the system should suggest that rather than just leaving them stuck. If there isn’t a workable option, then it should point them to contact support or a sales representative.

We’d need the usual protections around customer data and payment handling, so sensitive details should be handled securely and only collected when necessary. Checkout should also make the warranty and consumer sales information clear before purchase, especially for regulated products or anything with special return conditions. If a product has restrictions or if certain information can’t legally be shown in a promotional way, then it should be presented carefully and in the right context rather than hidden completely.

We should always prefer the latest live data for inventory, price, and order status, and make it clear when something is changing or only temporarily reserved. If there’s a mismatch, the system should avoid promising stock or pricing that hasn’t been confirmed, and it should show the customer the final confirmed value at checkout or in their order confirmation. If a detail is time-sensitive, I’d want it labeled as current at the time of viewing so we can explain any later changes.

We’d allow backorders only for items where the business has agreed it’s acceptable and we expect more stock to come in, rather than for everything that’s out of stock. If we offer it, the customer should be told clearly that fulfilment is delayed and given an estimated timing if we have one, but we shouldn’t promise an exact date unless it’s confirmed. If the timing is uncertain, we should say that follow-up may be needed and keep them updated through the order status.

We should tell them exactly which component or rule is causing the problem, in plain language, so they can see what needs to change. If we know a compatible option that meets the same need, we should offer that as the first alternative. If there isn’t a valid substitute, or the configuration is too complex to resolve automatically, then we should direct them to support or a sales person.

We’d want to standardize obvious things like product names, categories, units, and formatting so the catalogue is consistent across the new store. Any duplicate, outdated, or incomplete content should be cleaned up or removed if it can’t be reliably corrected. If something doesn’t fit the new structure and we can’t map it safely, I’d rather hold it back for review than force it into the store.

Yes, for borderline records I’d want human review rather than automatic decisions, especially if the item is incomplete but still potentially valuable. If the system can confidently standardize or map the data, then it can do that automatically, but anything ambiguous should be flagged for a person to check. We should only drop records automatically when they are clearly unusable, like obvious duplicates, corrupted entries, or content that fails basic validation.

We’d normally treat the current product management records as the main source of truth for core product data, because that’s what the business already controls. Marketing files can override things like descriptions, images, and campaign copy if they’re the approved version, and supplier files can be trusted for technical specs or component details when they’re more current. If there’s a conflict in core commercial data like price or availability, I’d expect that to stay with the store’s controlled records rather than being overwritten automatically.

We should do maintenance as late at night as practical, ideally outside normal trading hours, so customer impact is minimal. Weekends and public holidays should be avoided unless it’s urgent, because those are often busy periods or times when staff coverage is limited. If a change must affect customers, we should give advance notice and keep downtime as short as possible, but I’d need to check with the business on the exact notice period and maximum outage we can tolerate.

During those peak periods, slower response times really shouldn’t be something we plan to accept, because customers will abandon the site if browsing and search feel sluggish. We should scale up capacity ahead of expected peaks where possible, and protect the customer experience rather than letting traffic overwhelm the store. If needed, we can use throttling or other controls to keep the system stable, but I’d still want the main customer-facing functions to remain responsive.

I don’t have fixed numeric thresholds yet, but the trigger should be based on observed traffic trends and planned events rather than waiting for the site to degrade. Throttling should only be used as a last resort to protect stability, and mainly for non-essential or heavy background actions. The functions that really must stay responsive are product search, category browsing, product detail pages, and the ability to add to cart or start a configuration, because those are the core shopping actions.

If we start seeing response times climb, search results lag, or errors spike on the main shopping pages, that would be a strong sign to protect the site before the customer experience gets worse. I’d also use known event pressure, like a promotion going live or a holiday rush, as a reason to limit non-essential activity if our monitoring shows the store is getting close to capacity. The key condition is that core shopping functions must stay usable, so anything that’s consuming resources without directly serving customers is what we’d throttle first.

The first things to slow down would be non-customer-facing jobs like catalog imports, report generation, image processing, and any batch updates that can wait. I’d be cautious about pausing anything tied to order handling, payment confirmation, or inventory sync, because those affect live transactions and should keep running. If we’re near capacity, I’d rather defer nice-to-have background work than interrupt anything that could impact an active customer order.

Anything directly supporting an active order should keep running normally, especially payment confirmation, order creation, and inventory reservation or release. If a task is not needed to complete the transaction immediately, then it can usually be delayed or retried later in a controlled way. For the lighter retry approach, I’d expect us to verify with the team which jobs can safely queue without risking duplicate orders or stock mismatches.

We should expect the storefront to work properly on both mobile and desktop, but the layout can be adapted to suit the screen size. On mobile, the priority should be quick browsing, clear product details, and an easy checkout flow without too much clutter, while desktop can show more information at once. The purchase flow should be consistent between both, even if the presentation changes a bit to make it easier to use.

Yes, on mobile we’d likely simplify some things so the customer isn’t overwhelmed, especially long product descriptions, comparison tables, and large configuration panels. The actual checkout steps should stay essentially the same, but the screens may need to be broken up more cleanly or shown one step at a time. I wouldn’t want important details hidden completely, though; they can be collapsed or tucked behind expandable sections as long as customers can still find them easily.

Yes, I’d consider customer account creation and login a must-have, along with order confirmation and basic order history so customers can track what they bought. We’d also want a contact or support path on day one in case someone has an issue during purchase. I’m not sure we need the full range of extras like wish lists or reviews at launch, so those could probably wait.

Yes, payment processing and inventory integration would need to be in place before we can really go live, because those are core to taking orders correctly. We’d also need content and product data loaded and reviewed, otherwise the store won’t have anything useful to sell. If any of those are late, I’d prioritize the checkout and catalog basics first and push less critical features back.

We’d need inventory and pricing to be synchronized closely enough that customers aren’t shown stock or prices that are obviously wrong. If a sync is delayed or the data looks bad, I’d rather the store fail safely by hiding the affected item or marking it unavailable than let someone place an order on incorrect information. For launch, I’d want a clear fallback to the last verified data, but if that’s too stale, then we should block checkout on those items until the source system is healthy again.

If the last verified value is still recent enough to be trusted, we can show it, but it should be clearly treated as current only for a short window. Once it gets too old, I’d rather hide the item from sale or at least mark it unavailable than risk a bad order. If the item is visible but checkout depends on a live stock or price check, then checkout should be blocked for that item until the data is confirmed.

Before launch, only a small internal team should be able to publish or change storefront content and product data, probably product, merchandising, and admin staff. I’d want a review or approval step for anything customer-facing, especially prices, product descriptions, and promotional content, so mistakes don’t go live by accident. Simple operational updates might go straight through if they’re low risk, but anything that affects sales should be checked first.

Low-risk changes would be things like fixing typos, updating a product image, or correcting non-pricing descriptive text, and those could go live immediately if they don’t affect the buying decision. Anything that changes price, availability, configuration options, or the wording of promotional claims should require approval. If a change is small but could still confuse a customer or affect the order, I’d lean toward review before it publishes.

Yes, definitely. If the text is part of a legal disclaimer, warranty statement, or a regulated product description, even a small correction should be reviewed first. The same goes for brand-sensitive images or anything tied to a manufacturer’s approved marketing material, because we can’t just change those freely.

Yes, anything promotional, legally sensitive, or manufacturer-controlled should go through manual review before it’s published after migration. That includes warranties, compliance statements, pricing banners, and any copied marketing copy or images from suppliers. Even if the import is automated, I’d want those items checked by a person before they become visible to customers.

On day one, I’d prefer to allow guest checkout so customers can buy quickly without having to create an account first. We should require an account only if something truly depends on it, like accessing order history, saved configurations, or warranty registration later on. If login or account setup fails and the customer is otherwise ready to buy, that should not block the purchase unless the selected service absolutely needs the account.

On day one, customers should at least get a confirmation screen and email with the order number, items ordered, total, shipping choice, and expected delivery or processing status if we have it. In the account area, they should be able to see basic recent order history and current status, but not unnecessary personal data beyond what’s needed to identify and track the order. I’d keep history limited to the customer’s own orders and avoid exposing internal notes, payment details, or anything sensitive.

Yes, we should mask most of the shipping address and never show full payment details in order history. For cancelled, returned, or refunded orders, the customer should still see the order, but the status and a simple reason or outcome are enough; internal handling notes should stay hidden. If there are account types with special access, like staff or business accounts, that may change, but for normal shoppers I’d keep it very limited and privacy-focused.
